lines: A team wants to filter their dashboard by production batch, so they add one new label to every sensor reading.
Within a day, the metrics server's memory climbs far past what it normally uses, and the process gets killed outright.
The change itself was a single line.
Two readings only count as the exact same series if every one of their labels matches, all at once.
Change the value of even a single label, or add a label that wasn't there a moment ago, and the result isn't the old series continuing.
It's a brand new series, starting from nothing.
Multiply every label's distinct values together and the worst-case series count comes out large.
The plant's real series count comes from which sensors are genuinely fitted to which piece of equipment, which is far more constrained than that.
The real number lands well below the worst case, simply because the plant doesn't actually use every possible combination.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal answers it.
A query names several labels at once, say one particular site and one particular kind of sensor.
Does answering that query mean checking every single series the system knows about, one at a time?
answer: An index already holds exactly which series carry a given label, so the system can go straight to that short list instead of inspecting every series it has.

lines: Take the sorted list of series matching one label and the sorted list matching another, and merge the two lists together.
Wherever both lists agree on a series, that series matches the whole query — and the rest of the system's series were never even touched.
A pattern-based matcher doesn't get this shortcut at all. With no ready-made list of its own, it has to check every series directly.
Give every single sensor series its own batch label, with no limit on how many different batches can exist.
The series count doesn't grow by some fixed amount — it multiplies by however many distinct batches actually show up.
A label with no bound on its possible values has no bound on how many series it can ultimately create.
Store every reading as an ordinary row in a column-oriented table instead of as its own tracked series.
In that model, the same batch label is just another column sitting next to the reading, nothing more special than that.
There's no per-series structure for it to blow up — only a scan across rows that simply takes a bit longer as the table grows.
A series is entirely defined by its full set of labels, nothing more and nothing less.
An index built around that identity helps an exact-match query enormously, and offers a pattern-matching query almost nothing.
An unbounded label multiplies series count directly, a column-oriented model trades that index away for a scan instead, and a batch ID belongs in a table of facts, not inside a series' own identity.
One more case worth reasoning through before moving on.
The team that added the batch label wants to know exactly why their memory usage exploded, not just that it did.
Given the rule that a series is exactly its label set, can the new series count be stated precisely, with nothing left to guess?
answer: Because a series is nothing more than its labels, adding one new label with a known number of distinct values multiplies the prior series count by that exact number, with no estimation required.
